name: Road from London through Barnet to the fork (Great North Road)
summary: The main road north from London climbed Barnet Hill, ran through the market town past its chapel, and crossed Hadley Green to a fork where the Hadley Highstone now stands. Both armies came this way.
uncertainty: Drawn on the line of the modern A1000. The route is medieval, but its exact course and width in 1471 are not mapped by any source earlier than Ogilby (1675); Barnet Hill was cut down and embanked in 1823, and across the greens the road was a broad unfenced track, not a made carriageway. The obelisk at the fork dates from 1740 and is not shown.

name: St Albans road (now Kitts End Road)
summary: The road from London to St Albans, the Midlands and the north-west: the left-hand branch at the fork, running north-west past Kitts End to Dancers Hill. In 1471 this was the great road, and Warwick's army had marched down it from St Albans; today it is a country lane.
uncertainty: A St Albans road through South Mimms is recorded about 1220 and a document of 1479 puts it on or near this line between Kitts End and Dancers Hill; Ogilby's survey of 1675 is the first to show the course exactly, and it then followed the modern lane almost exactly. Its line in 1471 is therefore very probably this one but is not directly attested. Where it crossed open common it may have been up to 100 m wide.

name: Hatfield road (later the Great North Road)
summary: The right-hand branch at the fork, heading north-east to Potters Bar, Hatfield and the north along the edge of Enfield Chase.
uncertainty: Drawn on the modern A1000. The survey report argues that in the later Middle Ages this road ran just outside the Chase boundary bank and only shifted east into the Chase after the bank decayed, so the 1471 line was probably a little west of the one shown. It is first shown in detail in 1675; that it already existed as a major route in 1471 is an inference.

name: Wood Street (road west to Barnet Common)
summary: The lane branching west at Barnet chapel, widening as a drove towards Barnet Common.
uncertainty: Line taken from the modern street. Its medieval existence is inferred from the town plan and later maps, not from a 15th-century record.

name: Lane from the green to Hadley church
summary: A lane from the main road across the east side of the green to the church at the edge of Enfield Chase.
uncertainty: Some way to the church must have existed, but this line is simply the modern Hadley Green Road; nothing documents the 15th-century lane.

name: Monken Mead Brook
summary: A small stream rising north of Hadley church and running east through a shallow valley inside Enfield Chase. One contemporary newsletter puts Edward's army in a hollow or marsh; this valley is the usual candidate.
uncertainty: The modern stream line. The valley floor is narrow and the survey report doubts that it held much marsh; a pond at its east end is early modern. Whether any part of either army stood here is unknown.

name: Stream at the head of Margery Mead
summary: A stream falling north-west from the Kitts End side of the ridge into the broad, flat valley called Margery Mead, which may have been marshy before modern drainage.
uncertainty: The modern watercourse. A document of 1479 mentions a brook on the heath in this area, which suggests heathland reached further this way than later maps show; the stream's medieval course is not recorded.

name: Gannick Bank (boundary of Enfield Chase)
summary: The bank and hedge that divided Enfield Chase from the commons outside it, running north from Hadley towards Potters Bar beside the Hatfield road. If it was still a substantial hedged bank in 1471 it would have been a serious obstacle on the east side of the field.
uncertainty: A perambulation of 1572 describes a hedge along this boundary and one of 1675 'a great bank'; part of the line was picked up by geophysics in Wrotham Park. Its state in 1471 is not recorded, and a claim of 1693 that the pale was pulled down at the battle is late and probably unreliable. The line shown is approximate: it is set just east of the modern road, not taken from the survey plans.

name: A possible 'hedge-side' on the Hadley Green interpretation
summary: The Arrivall says Warwick's men were drawn up 'under a hedge-side' rather more than half a mile from Barnet. On the Hadley Green interpretation that hedge ran east–west near the north edge of the green; A. H. Burne thought he could identify it beside Old Fold.
uncertainty: The hedge of 1471 has never been identified and this line is a placeholder for one interpretation only. The survey report regards Burne's identification as unproven and notes that the same words fit the hedged closes north of Kicks End Common, or the hedge on the Chase boundary, at least as well.

name: Edge of the closes north of Kicks End Common
summary: Hedged closes lay north of the common by 1479. The survey report's simplest reading of the sources puts Warwick's line behind this boundary, facing south across the common, with a frontage of about 650 m between the two roads.
uncertainty: That enclosures existed here is documented (many are named in 1479, and roughly two thirds of the later Wrotham Park was already enclosed), but none is mapped before the 18th century, after the park was laid out. The line shown is a guess at the northern edge of the common.

name: Edge of the Old Fold estate beside the green
summary: Old Fold was a compact, fully hedged estate when first mapped in 1726, with its moated house at the eastern edge next to Hadley Green.
uncertainty: Whether the land west of the green was already enclosed in 1471 is not known; the report says so explicitly. This single hedge stands for that possibility.

name: Chapel of St John the Baptist, Chipping Barnet
summary: The town's church, standing at the angle where Wood Street leaves the High Street on the crest of the ridge, about 400 ft (122 m) above sea level. A chapel of St John is recorded here in 1361; it was largely rebuilt in the first half of the 15th century and was treated as a parish church by the time of the battle.
uncertainty: The building was almost entirely remodelled by Butterfield in 1875: the medieval nave arcades survive as the present north aisle, with parts of the old tower. The recorded old plan had a nave about 60 ft long and 16–19 ft wide and a chancel about 16 by 19 ft; aisle widths, heights and the tower's size are estimates. The split into three phases at 1420 and 1453 is a simplification of 'tower early 15th century, chancel about 1450, nave arcades and clerestory by John Beauchamp, who died in 1453'. Nothing is known of the form of the 14th-century chapel.

name: St Mary's church, Monken Hadley
summary: The parish church of Hadley, on the plateau at the edge of Enfield Chase east of the green. Hadley is listed as a parish church about 1175 and a hermitage 'in the park of Hadley' is recorded about 1136. The church that stood here on the day of the battle was replaced about 1494 by the present building, which carries that date on its west tower.
uncertainty: Nothing is known of the form of the church that stood in 1471 except that the later nave may preserve its plan; the small building shown before 1494 is a placeholder. The suggestion that the rebuilding followed damage in the battle is a modern guess with no evidence. The 1494 church is shown without the aisles (probably 16th century) and without its 19th-century additions; the walls are brown flint with stone dressings, for which the nearest available material is used. No dimensions were found in the sources; all are estimates. The site of the 12th-century hermitage is unknown.

name: Old Fold manor house (moated)
summary: A moated manor house at the north-west corner of Hadley Green, held by the Frowyk family of London merchants from soon after 1271 until 1527. A manor house is mentioned in 1310 and three sides of its moat survive beside the golf club house. It was certainly standing in 1471 and, on the Hadley Green interpretation, lay in or just behind Warwick's line.
uncertainty: Only the moat survives; nothing is known of the medieval house, so the timber-framed hall shown is a generic placeholder and the moat itself is not modelled. The position is that of the modern club buildings and may be 50 m out.

name: Chapel for the dead of the battle (site not proven)
summary: The Great Chronicle of London (about 1512) says the common dead were buried on the plain and that a little chapel was afterwards built there to remember their souls. A will suggests it was still in use in 1519–20; by Stow's day it had become a house. Since 1970 it has been identified with 'the Hermitage', a moated site on the former Kicks End Common, one arm of whose moat survives as a pond.
uncertainty: The chapel's existence is documented; its place is not. Geophysics and test pits at the moated site in 2017–19 confirmed the moat and a later house but found no chapel and no graves, and the report says the identification is 'still not beyond reasonable doubt'. The chronicle puts it half a mile from the town in one passage and a mile in another. The foundation date is unknown (shown here as built within a few years of 1471), and the building shown is a generic small chapel. It may have been a room in an existing hermitage, not a new building.

name: Registered battlefield area (Hadley Green)
summary: The area registered as the battlefield by English Heritage in 1995, following a National Army Museum report: Hadley Green, Old Fold and the ground north of Monken Hadley. Its northern edge is a little over half a mile from Barnet, matching the Arrivall's distance.
uncertainty: The outline is an approximation drawn for this model, not the official boundary (Historic England's entry could not be fetched). The 2015–18 survey called this location 'problematic': the green is only about 350 m wide, the road crosses it north–south so the armies could not have stood on opposite sides of it as one account says, there is no hollow for Edward's line, and the putative chapel lies well to the north. It has not been disproved; much of it is built over or golf course and has never been systematically searched.

name: Kitts End: the 2015–18 survey's alternative site
summary: The former Kicks End Common and its surroundings, between the St Albans and Hatfield roads north of the fork: a level hilltop of open common, about 1.9 km from the Barnet boundary, edged by hedged closes on the north and the bank of Enfield Chase on the east, with the Monken Mead valley falling away to the south-east. The survey report judged that this ground 'most closely' fits the written accounts, and the putative battle chapel lies on it.
uncertainty: The outline is drawn for this model from the report's description. Metal-detecting here in 2015–18 recovered no clear battle scatter, so the suggestion rests on the documents and terrain alone; the report itself concludes 'we cannot accurately identify the battlefield' and considers six different deployments. Watson (2022) describes the best guess more loosely, as a circle of 1 km radius centred on Kitts End.

name: Lancastrian right (Oxford)
summary: Stand-in for the western wing of Warwick's army, which the sources agree overlapped and routed the king's left; its men chased the fugitives towards Barnet and, returning in the mist, were taken for enemies by their own side. That the Earl of Oxford led the attack is attested; that this was the 'right wing' is inference.
uncertainty: A stand-in, not a record. Its name, wing and commander are given by modern reconstruction. The wing-by-wing order of battle is a modern reconstruction from military convention and a few phrases in the Arrivall; the only chronicler to give a Lancastrian order (Hall, decades later) arranges it differently. The real numbers are unknown: contemporary figures contradict each other and modern figures of roughly 10,000 Yorkists and 15,000 Lancastrians are estimates. On those estimates one figure here stands for about two men. The position follows the registered-battlefield (Hadley Green) interpretation, which the 2015–18 survey found hard to square with the sources; frontage, depth, spacing and exact place are invented for legibility. No guns, archers, horses or reserves are distinguished, and the two colours are arbitrary tints, not liveries.

name: Lancastrian centre (Montagu)
summary: Stand-in for the middle of Warwick's line. Modern accounts put John Neville, Marquess Montagu, here and Warwick himself with a reserve behind; no contemporary source says where either stood. Both were killed.
uncertainty: A stand-in, not a record. Its name, wing and commander are given by modern reconstruction. name: Lancastrian left (Exeter)
summary: Stand-in for the eastern wing of Warwick's army, which the king's line overlapped. The Duke of Exeter was badly wounded and left for dead; his place on the left is a modern inference.

name: Yorkist left (Hastings)
summary: Stand-in for the western end of the king's line, which was overlapped, broken and driven back through Barnet towards London. Lord Hastings led the rearward, which later sources place here.
uncertainty: A stand-in, not a record. Its name, wing and commander are given by modern reconstruction. name: Yorkist centre (Edward IV)
summary: Stand-in for the king's own division. The Arrivall, written by a servant of the king, describes Edward fighting in the midst of the press.
uncertainty: A stand-in, not a record. Its name, wing and commander are given by modern reconstruction. name: Yorkist right (Gloucester)
summary: Stand-in for the eastern end of the king's line, which overlapped the enemy's. Richard, Duke of Gloucester, aged eighteen, led the vanguard, conventionally placed on the right.
uncertainty: A stand-in, not a record. Its name, wing and commander are given by modern reconstruction. name: Thames ford (line conjectural)
summary: A crossing of the Thames by wading. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle has Edmund 'go over at Brentford' and later 'ford over the Thames at Brentford' in 1016, so a usable ford existed. The county history thinks the lowest permanent ford on the Thames was probably at Old England, the low ground by the Brent mouth; that is where it is drawn.
uncertainty: The exact line is not known. It is drawn from Old England to the Kew bank because the county history and local historians favour that spot; a crossing a few hundred metres downstream, where the Kew ferry later ran from Ferry Lane, is just as possible. The place-name itself is usually taken to mean the ford over the Brent, not the Thames. Timber stakes found on the foreshore at Old England and at Brentford End were claimed by Montagu Sharpe as the defences Caesar met in 54 BCE, and the county history allows that they were 'perhaps used to defend the ford': the Caesar link is antiquarian tradition, the stakes are undated in the sources read, Wheeler doubted the identification in 1929, and none are shown. Depth, bed and width of the ford are guesses.

name: River Brent
summary: The tributary that gives Brentford its name, joining the Thames from the north. Alluvium lies along it and at its mouth.
uncertainty: The course is the modern river and canal line, generalised. Below Brentford Bridge the Brent was straightened between 1699 and 1760 and later canalised, so the bends drawn here are not the 11th-century ones, and a second mouth that once made an island of the Old England ground is not shown. Width is a guess.

name: Crossing of the Brent on the west road
summary: Where the road west from London crossed the Brent. The name Brentford, recorded from 705, is usually taken to mean this ford. A bridge is first recorded in 1224, long after this window, so a ford is shown.
uncertainty: The ford has not been found. It is placed at the modern Brentford Bridge; the local history society thinks the early crossing 'probably lay near the present bridge site' and that the first wooden bridge may have been a little upstream. Whether a timber bridge already stood here in the 11th century is not known.

name: Road from London (later Brentford High Street)
summary: The main road from London to the west, successor to the Roman road to Silchester, running along the gravel just above the Thames to the Brent crossing.
uncertainty: The Roman road from London to Silchester and the west ran through Brentford from the late 1st century, with Roman buildings mainly just north of the modern High Street, but the county history says its line did not survive; the present High Street alignment is recorded only by the late 14th century. The line drawn is the modern High Street and London Road, generalised. That a through road was in use in 1016 is an inference from the place's role as a crossing, not a recorded fact, and its surface and width are guesses.

name: Road to the west (towards Staines)
summary: The same road beyond the Brent, through the later Brentford End towards Hounslow and Staines. The county history calls the London to Staines road probably the oldest man-made feature of the district.
uncertainty: The Roman road from London to Silchester and the west ran through Brentford from the late 1st century, with Roman buildings mainly just north of the modern High Street, but the county history says its line did not survive; the present High Street alignment is recorded only by the late 14th century. The line drawn is the modern High Street and London Road, generalised. That a through road was in use in 1016 is an inference from the place's role as a crossing, not a recorded fact, and its surface and width are guesses.

name: Track to the Thames ford (conjectural)
summary: A way from the west road to the head of the Thames ford, keeping west and south of the Brent's last bend.
uncertainty: Invented to connect the road with the ford as drawn. No such track is recorded or excavated, and if the ford lay elsewhere the approach did too.

name: Arable north of the road (conjectural)
summary: Ploughed strips on the brickearth and gravel above the road, standing for the farmland of the bishop of London's manor.
uncertainty: Open fields north and south of the highway at Old Brentford are first described in 1383. Whether the ground was laid out in strips, or ploughed at all, three and a half centuries earlier is not known; the outline, strip direction and spacing are invented.

name: Arable west of the Brent (conjectural)
summary: Ploughed strips south of the west road, standing for the large arable of the manor of Isleworth, which Domesday Book credits with land for 55 ploughs.
uncertainty: Domesday gives the size of the manor's arable in 1086, not where it lay; Isleworth village is over a kilometre to the south. The outline, strip direction and spacing are invented.

name: Fishing boats (illustrative)
summary: A few small boats off Old Brentford. A Thames fishery at Brentford existed by 996, when the king granted half of it to Winchester; later records speak of weirs.
uncertainty: The fishery is documented; the boats are not. Their number, place and form are illustrative, and the weir or fish traps the fishery probably used cannot be drawn with the kinds available.

name: Possible crossing, 1016 (conjectural)
summary: A shaded band over the ford as drawn: one place where Edmund's army may have crossed the Thames in 1016.
uncertainty: Invented for the staging. The Chronicle says only that the king 'went over at Brentford'. The band marks the ford line preferred by the county history, not a located crossing; see the second band downstream.

name: Another possible crossing, 1016 (conjectural)
summary: A second shaded band, on the line of the later Kew ferry from Old Brentford, shown to make plain that the crossing place is not known.
uncertainty: Invented for the staging. A ferry to Kew, probably from Ferry Lane, is recorded by the 16th century; nothing shows a ford there in 1016. The band is here only as an alternative to the first.

name: Possible Danish position, 1016 (conjectural)
summary: A shaded area on the Surrey bank where the Danish army may have stood. The Chronicle's wording, that Edmund crossed and then fought, is usually read as putting the fight south of the river, and the county history (citing Stenton) says it was fought on the south bank.
uncertainty: Invented for the staging. No source gives the Danish position. The south bank is an inference from one sentence; a skaldic poem has been read as implying fighting on both banks (not checked here). The area's place, size and shape are arbitrary.

name: Edmund's army (stand-in figures)
summary: A block of plain figures at the Middlesex end of the ford, standing for the English army that crossed the Thames here under King Edmund in 1016.
uncertainty: Invented for the staging. The size of Edmund's army is not recorded: 1,200 figures are drawn so that the block can be seen, and a figure does not stand for any number of men. Its place, formation and facing are arbitrary, and whether the army crossed in one body is unknown. No arms, banners or named leaders are shown.

name: Englishmen ahead of the army (stand-in figures)
summary: A small loose group on the Surrey bank, standing for the men who, the Chronicle says, 'went before the main army with a design to plunder' and of whom many drowned.
uncertainty: Invented for the staging. The Chronicle does not say where these men were, how many they were, or whether they drowned at the ford, in pursuit or elsewhere; Stenton and Poole are reported to have argued that they fell in the fighting and did not drown (not checked here). The 150 loosely spaced figures and this spot are arbitrary. Nobody is shown drowning.

name: Danish army (stand-in figures)
summary: A block of plain figures on the Surrey bank, standing for the Danish army that Edmund fought and put to flight.
uncertainty: Invented for the staging. The size of the Danish force is not recorded (a modern figure of 8,000 to 12,000 has no contemporary basis): 1,000 figures are drawn so that the block can be seen. Whether Cnut was present, who commanded, where the army stood and which way it fled are all unknown. No ships are shown because none are mentioned at Brentford.

name: Roman bridge
summary: A timber bridge across the Thames on the Fish Street Hill line, the reason the town stood here. A probable timber pier base of the late 1st century was excavated near Pudding Lane in 1981.
uncertainty: No bridge of the 50s is directly dated: a crossing 'in place by AD 63' is inferred from the layout of the quays, and a fixed bridge 'built by c. 85–90' is Milne's reading of the pier base, whose identification is still only probable. The exact line, pier count, deck height and the date it went out of use are unknown.

name: First forum and basilica
summary: The first civic centre on Cornhill: a gravelled court with a basilica about 40 × 20 m. It stayed in use while the much larger second forum was built around it.
uncertainty: Dated 'late 70s or 80s' (MOLA, after the 2025 Gracechurch Street discovery). Only the basilica size is documented; the court dimensions and all heights are conjecture.

name: Second forum and basilica
summary: The great forum-basilica of Londinium, built around and over the first forum from about 100 CE; the basilica ran along its north side.
uncertainty: Plan known from scattered excavations. The c. 167 m square figure comes only from a secondary lead and was not verified; every height is conjecture. Marsden argues older models wrongly added inner porticoes and a cross-walkway (not shown here).

name: Amphitheatre
summary: An oval arena beneath today's Guildhall Yard: built in timber about 74 CE and rebuilt shortly after 120 with a masonry arena wall and entrances. The seating was always timber.
uncertainty: Only the eastern end has been excavated. 'Over 100 m long' and a capacity of about 7,000 are the only verified figures; arena axes and seating height are estimates.

name: Plantation Place fort
summary: An earth-and-timber fort of about 1.5 hectares built on Cornhill around 63 CE, soon after the Boudican revolt: the main physical evidence for the town's military-led recovery.
uncertainty: Known from one excavated corner; the rectangle shown is a schematic 1.5 ha outline, and the timber wall stands in for turf-and-timber ramparts about 3 m high. End date approximate.

name: Cripplegate fort
summary: A stone-walled fort of about 4.5 hectares on the north-west edge of the town, built about 120. It was probably out of use as a fort by the later 2nd century; its north and west walls were built into the city wall about 200.
uncertainty: Internal buildings are barely known and are not shown. The side lengths used (about 220 × 215 m) are unverified. The walls are shown standing until 200 although the garrison had probably gone decades earlier.

name: City wall
summary: The landward wall, about 3 km long, 2–2.6 m thick and about 6.4 m high, built of Kentish ragstone c. 190–225 and enclosing some 134 hectares. It set the limits of the city for the next 1,400 years.
uncertainty: Condition between the 5th and 9th centuries is poorly documented; the weathered state shown is illustrative. Gate forms and tower spacing are schematic: the real eastern bastions are late Roman and the western ones medieval. The westward extension around Blackfriars (1282–1310) is not modelled.

name: Riverside wall
summary: A wall about 1,700 m long added along the river front c. 255–275 on the line of Thames Street, closing the circuit. Its eastern end was strengthened as late as c. 388–402, parts still stood in the late 9th century, and it had gone by the 12th.
uncertainty: Its full line and the pace of its collapse are only partly known; the slow decay shown is illustrative.

name: Cannon Street riverside complex ('governor's palace')
summary: A large terraced riverside complex with courts and an ornamental pool under Cannon Street station, formerly called the governor's palace.
uncertainty: Its function, and whether it was one building at all, are disputed; the western range is entirely hypothetical and the c. 130 × 100 m extent is from secondary sources. The single symmetrical courtyard shown is a placeholder.

name: Huggin Hill baths
summary: A large public bath-house terraced into the hillside above the river.
uncertainty: Only 'late 1st century' could be verified for construction; demolition c. 180–200 is unverified. Elevation is reconstruction.

name: Temple of Mithras
summary: A small aisled temple on the east bank of the Walbrook, built c. 240–250 with its apse to the west; converted, probably to Bacchus, in the early 4th century. Found in 1954.
uncertainty: Roof form and height are reconstruction; the 18 × 8 m plan is from secondary sources.

name: Road to the bridge from the south (Borough High Street line)
summary: The approach road across the Southwark islands, where the roads from the Kent coast and the south met before the bridge.
uncertainty: Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Road north (Bishopsgate line)
summary: The road from the bridge past the forum and north towards Lincoln and York.
uncertainty: Use of the stretch inside the walls between the 5th and 9th centuries is uncertain. Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Main east–west Roman street
summary: The principal street of Londinium, running east–west north of the Walbrook crossing.
uncertainty: Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Cheapside – Cornhill
summary: The market street ('ceap') of the re-established Saxon city, the spine of the medieval street plan.
uncertainty: The date at which the late Saxon street grid was laid out is debated (late 9th to 10th century).

name: Road west (Holborn line)
summary: The Roman road west from Newgate towards Silchester, still a main road in 1625.
uncertainty: Line simplified; the internal street grid was only partly regular.

name: Fleet Street – Strand – King Street
summary: The road along the river terrace from Ludgate through Lundenwic to Westminster.
uncertainty: Probably of Roman origin, but that is not proven for its whole length.

name: Walbrook stream
summary: The stream that divided the Roman and medieval city. Progressively built over and culverted; gone from view by the late 16th century.
uncertainty: No single date exists for the covering; Stow (1598) describes it as wholly vaulted over. The gradual narrowing shown is illustrative.

name: River Fleet
summary: A tributary entering the Thames at Blackfriars; an open, increasingly foul river throughout this period.
uncertainty: It silted and narrowed from the 13th century; the constant width shown is a simplification.

name: St Paul's Cathedral
summary: A cathedral has stood on Ludgate Hill since 604. The medieval building, 'Old St Paul's', was one of the longest churches in Europe and carried a very tall timber spire until 1561.
uncertainty: Nothing is known of the form of the Anglo-Saxon churches; the small buildings shown before 1087 are placeholders. Overall length 586 ft (about 179 m) is documented. Published spire heights range from about 122 to 158 m (149 m is the traditional figure); the model uses about 144 m and no figure is a reliable measurement.

name: Queenhithe
summary: A trading shore from the late 880s ('Æthelred's Hythe', first charter 889): at first an open beach market, with low timber revetments from the late 10th century and embankments dated 1021 and 1045. The main dock above the bridge through the Middle Ages.
uncertainty: The beach-market phase (c. 886–970) had no built quay and is not modelled; the timber dock shown is generic.

name: Late Saxon and Norman timber bridge
summary: A timber bridge existed again by about 1000 CE and was repaired or rebuilt several times before the stone bridge replaced it.
uncertainty: Its exact line, form and the number of rebuildings are not known; the model is generic.

name: Old London Bridge
summary: The stone bridge of 19 arches and a drawbridge opening, begun in 1176 and finished in 1209, about 276 m long and only about 6 m wide, lined with houses, with a chapel on its central pier and a fortified gate at the Southwark end.
uncertainty: Length 276 m follows MOLA (the traditional figure is 926 ft, about 282 m). The deck height above the water is undocumented and the 8 m used is an assumption. Individual pier, arch and starling sizes are generated, not measured. Five arches collapsed in the winter of 1281–82 and two (with the Stone Gate) in January 1437; those repairs are not animated.

name: Houses on London Bridge
summary: Houses stood on the bridge from soon after it was finished: about 140 by 1358 and about 130 in the 16th century, overhanging the river on both sides of a roadway only about 4 m wide and bridging it in places.
uncertainty: No house is individually documented before the 16th–17th century views, and those disagree in detail. Number of storeys before the 15th century is conjectural.

name: Chapel of St Thomas on the Bridge
summary: A two-storey chapel on the large central pier, dedicated to Thomas Becket. Rebuilt 1387–96; closed in 1548 and turned into a house, shop and warehouse.
uncertainty: Dimensions are not documented; the form follows later views.

name: Great Stone Gate
summary: The fortified gate at the Southwark end of the bridge. After 1577 the heads of traitors were displayed here.
uncertainty: Dimensions undocumented.

name: Drawbridge Gate
summary: A gate tower beside the drawbridge, seventh opening from the Southwark end. Demolished in 1577 and replaced by Nonsuch House.
uncertainty: Dimensions undocumented. Traitors' heads were displayed on this tower until its demolition in 1577.

name: Nonsuch House
summary: A four-and-a-half-storey timber house with corner turrets and onion domes, built across the bridge in 1577–79 on the site of the drawbridge tower; its design is attributed to Lewis Stockett, Surveyor of the Queen's Works.
uncertainty: Footprint about 22.9 × 7.6 m in the Gerhold-based account; height undocumented, and no measured contemporary drawing exists. It is said by later tradition, unverified, to have been prefabricated in the Netherlands.

name: London Bridge waterworks
summary: Tide-driven waterwheels under the northernmost arches, set up by Peter Morris in 1581–82 to pump river water into the city.

name: St Magnus the Martyr
summary: The parish church at the north end of the bridge; every traveller crossing passed its door.
uncertainty: No firm earliest mention could be verified: 1067 rests on a suspect charter, so 'by the early 12th century' is used. No reliable image of the medieval building survives; the form and the date of enlargement are generic.

name: Fishmongers' Hall
summary: The riverside hall of the Fishmongers' Company, just upstream of the bridge, from 1434.
uncertainty: 1434 is the traditional date of acquisition and was not verified. Appearance before the 1640s views is conjectural.

name: St Olave, Southwark
summary: Church at the south bridge foot dedicated to St Olaf of Norway, in existence by the late 11th century.
uncertainty: In existence by the late 11th century; the medieval form is generic.

name: St Mary Overie (St Saviour's)
summary: Augustinian priory church at the Southwark bridge foot, refounded 1106, rebuilt in Gothic style after the fire of 1212. It became the parish church of St Saviour in 1540 and survives as Southwark Cathedral.

name: Winchester Palace
summary: The London house of the bishops of Winchester on Bankside, with a great hall whose rose-window gable still stands.

name: Billingsgate
summary: The dock and market below the bridge, in use by about 1000 CE.

name: Roman quays and warehouses
summary: Massive oak-timber quays with open-fronted warehouses behind, rebuilt further out into the river several times between the 1st and 3rd centuries.
uncertainty: The model shows one generalised quay line that follows the modelled bank; the real sequence had several distinct waterfronts advancing about 35 m in all (a secondary figure). Warehouses are generic.

name: Westminster Abbey
summary: Edward the Confessor's great church, consecrated in 1065, was replaced from 1245 by Henry III's Gothic abbey. The nave took until the early 16th century; the west towers were not built until the 18th century and are not shown.
uncertainty: The Confessor's church is known from excavation and the Bayeux Tapestry; its elevation is reconstruction.

name: Henry VII's Lady Chapel
summary: The Perpendicular Lady Chapel at the east end of Westminster Abbey.

name: Westminster Hall and Palace
summary: William II's great hall of 1097–99, the largest in England, given its hammerbeam roof in the 1390s. The royal palace grew around it.
uncertainty: The surrounding palace buildings are shown only as a generic range. The 73 × 20.5 m plan was seen only in secondary summaries; wall and roof heights are estimates.

name: Tower of London: the White Tower
summary: William the Conqueror's great stone keep in the south-east corner of the Roman walls, begun in the 1070s and complete by about 1100.
uncertainty: The turrets' onion-shaped caps date from the early 1530s; the model shows one form throughout.

name: Tower of London: inner curtain wall
summary: The towered inner curtain built mainly under Henry III.
uncertainty: Wall line simplified to a quadrilateral.

name: Tower of London: outer curtain and moat
summary: Edward I's outer curtain wall and moat, 1275–85, which gave the Tower its concentric form.
uncertainty: Wall line simplified to a quadrilateral; the moat (about 50 m wide) is not modelled.

name: Baynard's Castle (first)
summary: A Norman castle in the south-west corner of the city, demolished in 1213; the site passed to the Blackfriars.
uncertainty: Its plan and appearance are unknown. A generic small keep is shown. Slighted 1213; the site was absorbed by Blackfriars in 1276. Nearby Montfichet's Tower, equally undocumented, is not shown.

name: Baynard's Castle (riverside house)
summary: A great riverside house rebuilt after a fire in 1428 and remodelled as a royal residence by Henry VII about 1501.

name: Temple Church
summary: The Knights Templar's church with its round nave, consecrated in 1185; the chancel was added by 1240.

name: Blackfriars
summary: The Dominican friary built from 1276 between Ludgate and the river; the city wall was moved west to enclose it. Dissolved 1538; its church was pulled down and the buildings became houses and, later, an indoor playhouse.
uncertainty: Layout is schematic.

name: Greyfriars (Christ Church)
summary: The Franciscan friary by Newgate. Its great 14th-century church, about 90 m long, became the parish church of Christ Church after the Dissolution.

name: Austin Friars
summary: The Augustinian friary founded in 1253. After 1538 the nave was given to London's Dutch Protestant community (1550).

name: Holy Trinity Priory, Aldgate
summary: A rich Augustinian priory founded in 1108 just inside Aldgate; the first London house to be dissolved (1532), then largely pulled down for a mansion.

name: St Bartholomew's Priory and Hospital
summary: Founded by Rahere in 1123 beside Smithfield. After the Dissolution the nave was demolished and the choir kept as a parish church.

name: Charterhouse
summary: A Carthusian monastery founded in 1371 with a great cloister of individual cells; a courtier's mansion after 1545 and Sutton's Hospital from 1611.

name: Savoy Palace, later Savoy Hospital
summary: John of Gaunt's palace on the Strand, the grandest noble house in England, destroyed in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Henry VII's hospital was built on the ruins from 1505.
uncertainty: No reliable image of the palace exists; the model is generic.

name: Guildhall
summary: The city's great hall, rebuilt from 1411, standing over the buried Roman amphitheatre.
uncertainty: An earlier stone guildhall stood on the site from the 12th–13th century; it is not shown.

name: Leadenhall
summary: A quadrangular public granary and market built in the 1440s on the site of the Roman basilica.

name: Royal Exchange
summary: Thomas Gresham's bourse, built 1566–68 around an arcaded courtyard on the Antwerp model and named the Royal Exchange after Elizabeth I's visit in 1571.
uncertainty: No dimensions were found; the footprint is estimated.

name: Bridewell Palace
summary: Henry VIII's brick palace beside the Fleet, built 1515–23; given to the City in 1553 as a workhouse and prison.

name: York Place, later Whitehall Palace
summary: The archbishops of York's London house, seized by Henry VIII in 1529–30 and expanded into the largest palace in Europe, a sprawl of courts and galleries between the river and St James's Park.
uncertainty: Shown as generic courtyards; the real plan was irregular. The 'Holbein Gate' (c. 1531–32) and tiltyard are not separately modelled.

name: Banqueting House, Whitehall
summary: Inigo Jones's Palladian hall of 1619–22, the first fully classical building in London. It replaced a banqueting house of 1606–07 that burned in January 1619.

name: Somerset House
summary: Protector Somerset's Renaissance palace on the Strand, 1547–52; Denmark House under James I's queen.

name: Northampton House (Suffolk House from 1614)
summary: A Jacobean courtyard mansion with corner turrets at Charing Cross, built about 1605–09 for the Earl of Northampton; known as Northumberland House only later.
uncertainty: Strand front about 162 ft (49 m); depth and height are estimates.

name: Lambeth Palace
summary: The London residence of the archbishops of Canterbury since about 1200, on the marshy bank opposite Westminster.
uncertainty: Dates here are from general reference knowledge and were not checked against a fetched source in this research pass.

name: Bermondsey Abbey
summary: A Cluniac priory (later abbey) founded in 1082 on the Bermondsey eyot; dissolved 1538 and replaced by a mansion.
uncertainty: Dates here are from general reference knowledge and were not checked against a fetched source in this research pass.

name: Custom House
summary: The quay where duties were collected. A custom house stood at Wool Quay by 1377 and John Churchman built a new one in 1382.
uncertainty: An Elizabethan rebuilding in 1559 is often stated but could not be confirmed, and one scholarly lecture implies it did not happen as planned; the model therefore shows a single building throughout. Form generic.

name: The Steelyard
summary: The walled riverside base of the Hanseatic merchants, with its guildhall and warehouses. Its privileges were withdrawn in 1598 but the buildings stood.

name: The Rose playhouse
summary: Philip Henslowe's playhouse of 1587, the first on Bankside; its foundations were excavated in 1989.
uncertainty: Plan (14-sided, about 22 m) is from excavation; height is not documented.

name: The Swan playhouse
summary: Built about 1595 in Paris Garden; the subject of the only surviving sketch of an Elizabethan playhouse interior.
uncertainty: Size and number of sides are not documented; the model borrows the Globe estimate.

name: The Globe
summary: Built in 1599 from the timbers of the Theatre; burned on 29 June 1613 and rebuilt with a tiled roof by 1614.
uncertainty: Only a small arc of the foundations has been excavated: the roughly 30 m diameter and 20 sides are extrapolations (16–18 sides is also argued). Height is undocumented.

name: Bear Garden, later the Hope
summary: A baiting ring on Bankside, replaced in 1613–14 by the Hope, a dual-purpose playhouse and baiting house.
uncertainty: Sizes are estimates. Hollar's 1647 view swaps the labels of the Hope and the Globe.

name: City waterfront
summary: The built-up river frontage of the City: successive timber and later stone revetments pushed the bank out into the Thames, creating wharves between Thames Street and the water.
uncertainty: The model draws one continuous frontage that follows the modelled bank line. The real waterfront was a patchwork of separately owned wharves, inlets and stairs, and the pace of medieval reclamation is not reliably quantified.

name: Bankside and Southwark river wall
summary: The embanked south shore from Paris Garden past Winchester Palace to the bridge foot and St Olave's.
uncertainty: Dates of embankment are generalised; the line follows the modelled bank.

name: Roman shipping
summary: Sea-going and river vessels served the Roman port; wrecks of the period have been excavated at Blackfriars and County Hall.
uncertainty: Numbers and positions are illustrative. Vessel forms are generic.

name: Medieval river traffic
summary: The Thames was London's main highway. Period panoramas of the 16th and 17th centuries show it crowded with wherries and barges above the bridge and sea-going ships below it.
uncertainty: Numbers and positions are illustrative, and the boats do not move. Vessel forms are generic.

name: Olaf's ships at the bridge (saga tradition)
summary: Longships below the timber bridge, standing for the saga account of an attack on London Bridge in 1014.
uncertainty: The attack is known only from Norse verse and a saga written about 200 years later; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is silent. Number, position and form of the ships are invented for the staging, and the bridge is deliberately not shown collapsing.

name: Sarsen trilithon horseshoe
summary: Five sarsen trilithons (ten uprights, five lintels) in a horseshoe about 13.7 m across, open to the north-east; the tallest, the Great Trilithon at the south-west, stood about 7 m above ground. Drawn from the stone catalogue: stone positions and sizes are surveyed from what stands today, the original complete form is reconstructed from them.
uncertainty: Which stones stood, leaned, lay or had been taken by 1625 is not recorded; the 1625 state is reasoned backwards from Stukeley (1720s), Wood (1740) and Barclay (1895). One tradition (John Aubrey, c. 1665-93) ties the fall of the Great Trilithon to the Duke of Buckingham's digging in 1620; it is a report 45 years later, not a dated observation, and the 1625 phase shows stones 55 and 156 fallen on that basis. The middle trilithon heights are catalogue estimates. The fresh-dressed to weathered handover at 2400 BCE (about 120 years) is conjectural: no source dates the weathering of sarsen surfaces. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Sarsen circle and lintels
summary: The outer ring of thirty sarsen uprights (about 4.1 m high, 2.1 m wide) carrying a continuous ring of thirty lintels about 4.9 m above ground; outer diameter about 29.6 m. Seventeen uprights and six lintels stand today. The complete ring shown in the built phases is a reconstruction.
uncertainty: Whether the circle was ever complete is unresolved. Darvill (2012) counts uprights 13, 17, 18, 20 and 24 and 24 lintels as missing and favours historic robbing (the sockets of 13 and 20 are recorded); Ashbee (1998) argued it was never finished; drought parchmarks in 2013 between stones 16 and 21 (Banton et al. 2014) may be stoneholes where expected uprights should be, which would favour a complete circle. The built phases show the missing uprights 13, 17, 18, 20 and 24 and their lintels as HYPOTHETICAL stones. The 1625 phase shows the circle as catalogued (state reasoned from the 1720s surveys). The fresh-to-weathered handover at 2400 BCE is conjectural. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Bluestones in the Aubrey Holes (contested)
summary: On Parker Pearson's interpretation the 56 Aubrey Holes held bluestones from about 3000 BCE, so Stonehenge's first stones were a ring about 87 m across just inside the bank. Shown as 56 small standing bluestones.
uncertainty: CONTESTED. The 2008 re-excavation of Aubrey Hole 7 revived Hawley's idea of stones in the holes, and Parker Pearson (2020-22) argues for stones from c. 3000 BCE; Darvill (2022) holds that they held timber posts or nothing. No stone survives in situ. The stone sizes, count in use and the date of removal (here the start of Stage 2, 2620 BCE) are modelled, not recorded. The Aubrey Holes are drawn as open pits by their own landmark regardless of this reading.

name: Q and R bluestone double arc (Stage 2)
summary: A double ring of bluestones between the trilithons and the sarsen circle, set in the Q and R holes (paired 'dumbbell' sockets on the east, a single line on the south and west). Drawn as two parametric rings of 54 stones in all.
uncertainty: The sockets are excavated (Atkinson, Darvill); the stones, their heights and the real pattern are not. Count 50-80 in the sources; 54 drawn. Atkinson thought the circle unfinished; Parker Pearson prefers a single arc on the S and W; Darvill prefers erosion of the evidence. The two rings are circular approximations of an irregular pattern. End date: Darvill places the dismantling at the start of Stage 4 (2280 BCE), after the central circle (Stage 3) was added; the lead's brief suggested 2480-2400 BCE: Darvill's account is followed here.

name: Central bluestone circle (Stage 3) and bluestone oval (Stage 4)
summary: Two bluestone settings inside the trilithons, one after the other: a small central circle in Stage 3 and the oval of about 25 stones in Stage 4, which later became the horseshoe. Both are parametric stand-ins.
uncertainty: Stage 3: only an arc of five stoneholes is evidenced; that it was a full circle, its radius and its stones are conjectural (a ring of 18 is drawn). Stage 4: the oval of c. 24-25 stones is inferred from stoneholes; its exact shape, orientation (here the axis, 49.9 degrees) and stone sizes are modelled, and the 25 positions lie on an ellipse of 5.6 x 4.4 m semi-axes chosen to fit inside the trilithons. Dates: Stage 3 2480-2280 BCE, Stage 4 2280-2020 BCE (oval 2205-1920 BCE at 95%; modelled 2060 BCE). Nothing stands in this setting between 2280 and 2120 BCE in the model: that gap is a convention covering dismantling and rebuilding.

name: Outer bluestone circle
summary: The bluestone circle between the trilithons and the sarsen circle, about 22 m across (radius 11 m), of 40-60 stones when complete (Stage 4). Nineteen stone positions are catalogued from the surviving stones and stumps; the complete ring is drawn as 60 parametric stones.
uncertainty: The original count is 40-60 (Darvill et al.), 60 drawn. Only part of the ring survives (7 standing, others fallen, stumps or buried); the 1625 phase uses the catalogue, whose positions for stones 33-36 and 37-44 are schematic (+/-10 to 20 degrees) and whose buried entries are known only from records of their stumps. Which of them stood, fell or had been removed by 1625 is not recorded: the complete-to-ruinous swap at year 1 CE is a convention. Darvill thinks at least seven oval stones were removed in Roman times; no stone of this ring is individually dated. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Bluestone horseshoe
summary: The bluestone horseshoe inside the trilithons, open to the north-east, of about 19 stones (Stage 5). Twelve positions are catalogued from surviving stones; the complete setting is drawn as 19 parametric stones.
uncertainty: DATE DISPUTED: Atkinson dates the horseshoe to the end of the third millennium BCE (Stage 5, 2020-1520; the EH chronology gives 2205-1920 BCE at 95% for the oval/horseshoe); Darvill thinks the removal of at least seven stones at the north end of the oval to make a horseshoe was 'highly likely' Roman. The 19 stones are a count from the literature, drawn on a regular arc of radius 5.0 m; the catalogue's positions for the survivors (r 4.2-6.2 m) are the better evidence. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Altar Stone
summary: A slab of green-grey sandstone about 4.9 x 1.0 x 0.5 m at the foot of the Great Trilithon, from outside southern Britain. Drawn lying flat at ground level.
uncertainty: Its date of placing is tentative (Darvill: Stage 2, perhaps any time before the Great Trilithon fell on it); its original posture (flat or upright) is not established; its source is unsettled. In 1625 it is shown broken (2-3 pieces, Stukeley 1723) beneath the fallen Great Trilithon: that depends on the unknown date of the fall (if the tradition of 1620 is wrong it lay whole). The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Station Stones
summary: Four small sarsens (91-94) in a rectangle just inside the bank. Two (91, 93) survive; the other two positions are marked by modern plaques at the findspots of their barrows.
uncertainty: The date is uncertain (the EH timeline puts them with the sarsens; Atkinson earlier). Stones 92 and 94 are placed from modern markers, +/-1.5-3 m, and stood in barrows; their forms are inferred from 91 and 93. 91 is shown fallen and 93 standing in 1625 (reasoned from 1771 and the 1720s). The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Slaughter Stone
summary: A fallen sarsen about 4.9 m long (6.1 m as catalogued when standing) in the north-east entrance, once standing there with companion stones D and E.
uncertainty: Whether it stood upright originally is inferred from its stonehole and Darvill's reconstruction of an entrance facade; D and E (removed in Stage 3) are not drawn. When it fell is not recorded: it lay flat in the 1720s. The 'Slaughter' name is 17th-century folklore. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Heel Stone (and stonehole 97)
summary: An unshaped sarsen about 4.7 m high, 77.4 m from the centre on the solstice axis, with a second stonehole (97) beside it.
uncertainty: It leans toward the circle today (the lean is not modelled); when it began to lean is unknown. Darvill gives two scenarios (96 added beside 97, or 97's stone moved to 96); the stone in 97 is inferred from the hole alone (marked hypothetical) and shown only in the built phase. The ditch round the Heel Stone was dug in late Stage 2 or early Stage 3 and is not drawn. The handover at year 1 CE is a CONVENTION, not a dated event: losses and falls between the end of use (c. 1500 BCE) and the first drawings (c. 1573 CE) are undated. Roman-period disturbance is recorded at the site, and nothing else is known of when individual stones fell or were taken.

name: Aubrey Holes
summary: Fifty-six chalk pits in a ring about 87 m across (circumference 271.6 m), just inside the bank, each about 1.06 m wide and 0.76 m deep on average. Cremations were inserted in their upper fills.
uncertainty: Count, ring and size are well attested; the function is not (stones, posts or neither: see the bluestone landmark). The holes may predate the ditch (the cremated woman beside hole 7 is 98% likely older). How long they stayed open and when they were filled are NOT known: the open phase to 2500 BCE and the filled dimples afterwards are a modelled convention. Only about 34 of the 56 were excavated.

name: Stonehenge ditch and bank
summary: A circular bank with an external ditch, about 110 m across overall, with a wide entrance to the north-east on the solstice axis and a smaller one to the south. Ditch dug with antler picks; re-cut in Stage 3. Drawn with the ditch centreline at radius 53 m.
uncertainty: The overall diameter (c. 110 m) is attested; the ditch and bank profile are NOT (width 5 m, bank 4 m wide and 1.8 m high are modelled; a hint of ditch 1.2-2.3 m deep and bank 5-6 m wide comes from a source I could not read). Entrance widths are not recorded (here 20 degrees NE, 14 degrees S, an unsourced visual choice; the S entrance azimuth is approximate). Whether the ditch was dug in segments is not stated in the sources read, so it is drawn continuous. The date of the re-cut (2350 BCE here) is only bracketed (after 2450-2230 BCE). The smaller outer bank (counterscarp) is inferred to be the re-cut spoil. Later erosion is not dated: the lowered bank from year 1 CE is a convention; by Stukeley's time bank and ditch were still visible.

name: Midsummer sunrise marker (computed)
summary: A computed marker for the Events menu: the direction of sunrise on the midsummer solstice seen from the centre of Stonehenge in 2500 BCE, azimuth 49.2 degrees. It is an analytical overlay, not a structure and not lighting. The lead computed the azimuth for 2500 BCE, latitude 51.179, obliquity 23.97 degrees, with the horizon assumed at 0.6 degrees.
uncertainty: The azimuth depends on the unknown horizon elevation (0-1 degree shifts it by about 1 degree), refraction and the choice of limb; no source gives a survey azimuth of the axis. Which solstice the builders intended is debated (Ruggles favours midwinter; Parker Pearson allows midsummer). Present only in 2500 BCE.

name: Midwinter sunset marker (computed)
summary: A computed marker for the Events menu: the direction of sunset on the midwinter solstice seen from the centre of Stonehenge in 2500 BCE, azimuth 230 degrees. It is an analytical overlay, not a structure and not lighting. The lead computed the azimuth for 2500 BCE, latitude 51.179, obliquity 23.97 degrees, with the horizon assumed at 0.6 degrees.
uncertainty: The azimuth depends on the unknown horizon elevation (0-1 degree shifts it by about 1 degree), refraction and the choice of limb; no source gives a survey azimuth of the axis. Which solstice the builders intended is debated (Ruggles favours midwinter; Parker Pearson allows midsummer). Present only in 2500 BCE.

name: Greater Stonehenge Cursus
summary: A great banked and ditched enclosure about 2.75 km long and about 100 m wide, running ENE (bearing 84.6 degrees) north of Stonehenge, closed at both ends. Earlier than the stones.
uncertainty: Length (2751 m, from the OSM outline) and width (about 100 m, 75-133 m on the outline; Wikipedia up to 150 m at the west) are surveyed from earthwork traces; bank height and width are NOT recorded anywhere I could read (bank 5 m wide, 0.8 m high are modelled), nor whether the banks were inside or outside the ditches. Antler dates: 3630-3375 BCE (west terminal ditch) with a possibly older pick (Thomas et al. 2009); EH says c. 3500 BCE; re-cuts are reported c. 2500 and 2000-1500 BCE and are not drawn. Three possible entrances (N and two S) are not drawn. The route is the OSM outline's axis, simplified.

name: Lesser Stonehenge Cursus
summary: A smaller banked and ditched enclosure about 420 m long and 40-60 m wide, running WSW-ENE about 750 m north-west of the west end of the Greater Cursus.
uncertainty: Known only as a cropmark ploughed flat since the Second World War: size from the OSM outline (422 x 40 m; Wikipedia c. 400 x 60 m), bank and ditch sizes modelled (bank 4 m wide, 0.6 m high, width 45 m between crests). Date: antler c. 3000 BCE (Wikipedia only), which conflicts with EH's 'centuries around 3500 BC'. Its state in 1625 is unknown.

name: Amesbury 42 long barrow
summary: A long barrow just beyond the east end of the Greater Cursus, aligned north-south, about 62 x 20 m with ditches 11 m wide (as surveyed), levelled by ploughing and now under a track.
uncertainty: Radiocarbon 3640-3370 BCE; whether the cursus or the barrow is older is unknown (EH). Original height unknown (0.29 m survives; 2.0 m drawn); the OSM outline is longer (81 m). Mound size is surveyed at the surviving earthwork (the mound is lower today than when built); which end was wider is not known.

name: Winterbourne Stoke 1 long barrow
summary: The Winterbourne Stoke Crossroads long barrow, 84 x 27 m and 3 m high, NE-SW, later the focus of a round-barrow cemetery.
uncertainty: No radiocarbon date: the date here is a generic placeholder for 4th-millennium BCE long barrows. Ditches 12 m wide are recorded (6 m drawn per ditch). Mound size is surveyed at the surviving earthwork (the mound is lower today than when built); which end was wider is not known.

name: Normanton Down long barrow (OSM-mapped mound)
summary: A small long barrow on Normanton Down, mapped as a 19 x 9 m mound (bearing 11 degrees). Probably one of the two or three small long barrows EH and Internet Archaeology list here.
uncertainty: Which of Wilsford 30, Amesbury 14 and Wilsford 13 this mapped mound is, is not established (it lies 450 m from the nearest of the two with published coordinates). The OSM outline shows only the surviving mound (19 x 9 m); drawn at 25 x 12 m, a modelled original. No date: placeholder. Mound size is surveyed at the surviving earthwork (the mound is lower today than when built); which end was wider is not known.

name: Wilsford 30 long barrow
summary: A long barrow on Normanton Down, 43 x 20 m and 2.3 m high, aligned west-east, with ditches about 4 m wide.
uncertainty: No date: placeholder for the 4th millennium BCE. A Neolithic mortuary enclosure lies south of one of the Normanton Down long barrows (Wikipedia, not drawn). Mound size is surveyed at the surviving earthwork (the mound is lower today than when built); which end was wider is not known.

name: Amesbury 14 long barrow
summary: A long barrow near Normanton Down, 33 x 18 m and 1.6 m high, aligned NNW-SSE.

name: Stonehenge Avenue
summary: A processional way of two parallel banks with outside ditches, from the north-east entrance of Stonehenge along the solstice axis for about 530 m, then curving east across Stonehenge Bottom and King Barrow Ridge and down to the River Avon at West Amesbury, about 2.7 km in all. Built in Stage 3.
uncertainty: Course: from the OSM tracing of the ditch-bounded polygons (good to about 5-10 m). The first 35 m (from the earthwork entrance to the start of the mapped polygons) and the last 190 m to the West Amesbury henge are straight EXTRAPOLATIONS. Width: corridor about 12 m between banks, ditches about 20 m apart (EH 2010; OSM polygons 23 m); bank size is modelled. Date: antler picks 2345-2200 BCE, Darvill 2430-2200 BCE; modelled 2315 BCE; built here 2400-2300. No earlier first stretch is attested in the sources read (Parker Pearson argues natural periglacial stripes under it were followed; this does not date a built Avenue). Banks were already low in 1625 (lowered from year 1 CE by convention); ploughing levelled much of it after Stukeley's time.

name: Durrington Walls henge
summary: The largest henge in Britain: a circular enclosure about 500 m across with a huge outer bank about 3 m high and a deep ditch, built c. 2480-2450 BCE over the line of an earlier ring of timber posts, beside the Neolithic village on the slope to the Avon.
uncertainty: Position (centre +/-60 m) and outline are an ELLIPSE (466 x 490 m, Gazetteer of Great Britain), NOT a surveyed outline. Ditch about 5.5 m deep, 18 m wide at the top, 7 m at the base (Wikipedia; Current Archaeology gives other figures); modelled ditch 14 m wide, bank 25 m wide and 3 m high (up to 30 m wide in Wikipedia). Entrances: sources CONFLICT (N, S and E, with N and S blocked 2-3 centuries later, per Current Archaeology; Wikipedia lists NW and SE). The first reading is drawn, with entrances 14 m wide (unsourced). In 1625 the earthwork is shown ploughed down (bank 1.8 m): that change is undated and a convention.

name: Durrington Walls timber ring (beneath the later bank)
summary: A great ring of up to about 300 timber posts, roughly 5 m apart, 440-450 m across, enclosing the valley and village before the henge bank was raised along the same line.
uncertainty: Post pits are found by radar and excavation; the post height (about 5 m, Current Archaeology; Wikipedia says 7 m and 1.5 m diameter) and whether the ring was a palisade or free-standing posts are inferred. It lasted at most about 50 years, then the posts were pulled and the sockets packed with chalk (the 2015 'standing stones' claim was refuted in 2016). Drawn as a circle of radius 222 m; the real line may be oval.

name: Durrington Walls Southern Circle (timber)
summary: A circular setting of concentric rings of timber posts inside the henge, oriented to midwinter sunrise (south-east), beside the settlement.
uncertainty: Position only +/-60-100 m (the Wikipedia text cannot be reconciled with the enclosure ellipse). Rings: the sources say four rings, later six; NO ring radii, post counts, sizes or heights are in anything read. The sizes drawn (six rings, outer ring 40 m across, posts 0.7 m thick and 5 m high) are borrowed by analogy from Woodhenge and are CONJECTURAL. Whether it was roofed is unknown. The end date is unknown; posts are shown rotting after 2400 BCE (a placeholder). It was not replaced by stone in anything read.

name: Durrington Walls Northern Circle (timber)
summary: A smaller timber circle found by Wainwright in 1966 just north of the Southern Circle.
uncertainty: Nothing is known of its rings, posts, date or end: the two rings of 9 and 12 m radius, 5 m posts and a position 90 m north of the Southern Circle are placeholders. Decay after 2400 BCE is a placeholder.

name: Woodhenge (six oval rings of timber posts)
summary: Six concentric oval rings of timber posts (168 post-holes; outer ring 43 x 40 m), inside a ditch and bank 110 m across overall, with a single north-east entrance, near Durrington Walls.
uncertainty: The 168 post-holes and the outer ring size are excavated. The split of posts between rings, the ring spacing, the post sizes and especially the HEIGHTS (up to 7.5 m, inferred) are modelled; whether the posts stood free, were roofed or lintelled is unknown (lintels are deliberately not drawn). The long-axis bearing of the ovals is not stated in anything read: 50 degrees (towards the NE entrance) is a visual choice. When the posts decayed or were removed is unknown: shown rotting 2350-2150 BCE as a placeholder, although the ditch is dated 2470-2000 BCE and use is reported c. 1800 BCE. Modern concrete markers are not shown.

name: Woodhenge ditch and bank
summary: The ditch (up to 12 m wide, 2.4 m deep) and bank (10 m wide, 1 m high) enclosing Woodhenge, 110 m across overall, with a north-east entrance.
uncertainty: Overall diameter, widths and heights are from Wikipedia; whether the bank lay outside the ditch is assumed (outer, as for a henge); the ditch radius (38 m) is derived from 110 m overall. Entrance width (20 degrees) is a visual choice. Ploughing and levelling are mentioned but undated; the low grassed bank in 1625 is a modelling choice.

name: Coneybury henge
summary: An oval ditched enclosure about 45 x 55 m south-east of Stonehenge, excavated in the 1980s; the ditch was about 4 m wide and 3 m deep. Levelled by ploughing.
uncertainty: NO absolute date was found: the 2700 BCE start is a placeholder (pottery from the early Neolithic to the Middle Bronze Age). Whether it had a bank, inside or outside, is not documented (none drawn). Orientation of the oval is unknown (drawn long axis east-west). The levelling is thought to be medieval ridge-and-furrow ploughing: shown decaying 1200-1500 CE as a placeholder. The Coneybury Anomaly pit (early Neolithic, 12 m NW) is not drawn.

name: West Amesbury henge and 'Bluestonehenge'
summary: On the Avon bank at the end of the Avenue: a circle of about 25 stones (probably bluestones, from the shape of the sockets), later removed, then a small henge (ditch about 25 m across, outer bank).
uncertainty: Only stone sockets survive; their stones are inferred to be bluestones, ring about 10 m across, up to about 27 sockets (25 drawn). Erection date UNCERTAIN (Wikipedia 3400-2500 BCE from two arrowheads; 3000 BCE is a guess); the stones were removed 2469-2286 BCE (antler dates), perhaps to Stonehenge (unproven); the ditch and outer bank c. 2400 BCE. 'Ditch about 25 m wide' is taken as the ring's diameter. Position is approximate (OSM: 'approximate location from photos').

name: Cuckoo Stone
summary: A squat sarsen set up in a pit between Woodhenge and Durrington Walls, with cremations around it c. 2000 BCE. It lies fallen today.
uncertainty: No dimensions are in the sources read: 1.8 x 1.2 m and 1.3 m high are INVENTED to suit 'squat'. It was erected before 2000 BCE (2800 BCE is a placeholder); a post first stood in the socket. When it fell is unknown, so it is drawn standing throughout; it may have fallen at any time before 1625.

name: Normanton Down barrows
summary: A cemetery of round barrows on the ridge south of Stonehenge, burials roughly 2600-1600 BCE; about 35 survived in 1957. 33 round barrows are drawn.
uncertainty: Burials span roughly 2600-1600 BCE; Wilsford G7 is probably 2000-1800 BCE. Bush Barrow has its own landmark. Barrow positions are from OpenStreetMap outlines; every FORM is generic (bowl) and the sizes are only the mapped outlines' equivalent circles (clamped to 8-40 m, heights assumed): OSM gives no bell, disc or saucer forms, and Wikipedia says Normanton Down has bells, many discs, a saucer and a pond without saying which. Which barrow was raised when within 2200-1500 BCE is not known: the three build phases assign each barrow to a period by a fixed pseudo-random rule, so the SEQUENCE shown is illustrative. Tier is set by the group's centre.

name: Vespasian's Camp hillfort
summary: An Iron Age hillfort of about 14 ha on a spur above the Avon, 730 m north-south, with a bank up to 40 m wide and 6 m above the ditch floor, a ditch 10 m wide and an outer counterscarp bank (defences 68 m wide in all).
uncertainty: The CONSTRUCTION DATE IS A PLACEHOLDER: nothing retrieved says more than 'Iron Age' (700-600 BCE shown). The ring is the OSM outline of the rampart, re-sampled to 24 points; no entrance gap is drawn (none known). Bank 25 m wide and 4 m high above ground are modelled from the dimensions quoted (6 m above the ditch floor); the counterscarp is not drawn. The name is Camden's (16th century), not Roman. A medieval road over the hilltop and the 18th-century landscaping are not drawn.

name: Amesbury Abbey (nunnery, then Fontevraud priory)
summary: A Benedictine nunnery said to be founded c. 979 by Queen Aelfthryth; dissolved by Henry II in 1177 and refounded as a Fontevraud priory; dissolved at the Dissolution (1539 or 1540) and demolished, the estate going to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford.
uncertainty: Dates: foundation c. 979, 1177 refoundation (Wikipedia); the Dissolution is given as 1540 (Amesbury article) while the brief says 1539: 1540 is used. The BUILDINGS are unknown: no plan, no precinct boundary (the geography notes give only a placeholder rectangle), and no source for the conventual church's form or position. The church here is a generic stand-in, placed beside the parish church (about 45 m west of it): the parish church St Mary and St Melor may itself be the surviving priory church (Wikipedia). The 979 church and the 1177 priory church are drawn identically because nothing says the fabric changed. The date of demolition after the Dissolution is unknown; shown decaying until 1580 as a placeholder.

name: Parish church of St Mary and St Melor, Amesbury
summary: The Grade I parish church of Amesbury, which may be the surviving priory church. It survived the demolition of the priory.
uncertainty: The sources read give no date for the building and no plan: shown from 1177 as a placeholder and drawn as a generic aisled church with a west tower (the real form and any 1625 alterations are not modelled). Whether it is the priory church or an earlier parish church is unresolved.

name: Amesbury Abbey house (Seymour, 16th century)
summary: After the Dissolution the Crown granted the estate to Edward Seymour, Earl of Hertford, whose family held it until 1675. A Seymour house stood here in the 16th century.
uncertainty: NO description, plan or date of any 16th-century house is in the sources read. The 1661 and 1834-40 mansions are later than the timeline. The position is the OSM point for the present Amesbury Abbey house, the form is a generic hall, and the 1560 date is a placeholder.

name: River Avon
summary: The Hampshire (Wiltshire) Avon flowing south from Bulford past Durrington and Amesbury, round Vespasian's Camp and West Amesbury, about 10 km of the river within the modelled area. The Avenue ends on its bank at West Amesbury.
uncertainty: The course is the MODERN centreline (OSM) with side channels and water meadows omitted; the prehistoric and medieval channel will have meandered differently, and the course was changed by water-meadow works. Width 10 m is an estimate, not tagged in OSM. Alder-hazel carr and sedge fringed the floodplain in the Neolithic and Bronze Age, and channel sedimentation rose with clearance c. 800-500 BCE (not modelled).

name: Roman building near the Cuckoo Stone
summary: Excavation south-west of the Cuckoo Stone found a small rectangular Roman building with coins, thought a probable shrine.
uncertainty: Only existence and rough position (south-west of the stone) are attested. Size (12 x 7 m), form, roof and the dates (100-410 CE) are PLACEHOLDERS; it is drawn as a generic hall. Other Roman-period activity (coins and pottery at the stones, a settlement near the Avon, arable colluviation) is not drawn.
